title: Best Sum of Pair Minimums
statement:
You get an array nums with an even number of integers. Split all of them into pairs, every number in exactly one pair. Each pair scores the smaller of its two numbers.

Return the largest possible total score over all pairs.

examples.why: Pair (2, 4) and (5, 9) for 2 + 5 = 7. Pairing the two biggest with the two smallest, (2, 9) and (4, 5), gives only 6.
Pairs (−7, −4) and (−2, 0) score −7 + −2. Negative totals are fine.

hints: The very smallest number scores no matter which partner it gets. Whose value does it waste?
The smallest number's partner never scores. To waste as little as possible, give it the second smallest number.
Sort and add every other element starting from index 0.

explain.intuition:
The smallest number is the minimum of whatever pair it lands in, so it always scores, and its partner never does. You want that wasted partner to be as small as possible, so pair the smallest with the second smallest. Remove both and the same argument repeats on what is left.

So after sorting, pairs are neighbours (0, 1), (2, 3), …, and the answer is the sum of the elements at even indexes. Because values sit in a small range, a counting sort makes it linear.
steps: For O(n + range): count each value, walk values from low to high, and add a value every time its running position is even.
pitfalls: Pairing the smallest with the largest to "balance" pairs. That wastes the largest number, as in the first example.
Sorting numbers with JavaScript's default sort(), which compares strings: -4 would land after -2.
In the counting version, resetting the even/odd position per value. Duplicates of one value can straddle pairs.

complexity.time: O(n log n), or O(n + range) with counting
complexity.space: O(1) extra after sorting, O(range) for counting

solutions.title: Try every pairing
solutions.idea: Pair the first remaining number with each other remaining number in turn and recurse. Exponential, only for tiny inputs.

solutions.title: Sort and take every other
solutions.idea: After sorting, neighbours pair up and the left one of each pair scores.

solutions.title: Counting sort
solutions.idea: Values lie in [−10 000, 10 000]. Count them, then walk the values in order, scoring each one that lands on an even position.

followups: Prove the greedy choice with an exchange argument: take any optimal pairing and show you can swap partners until the smallest two are together.
Split into groups of three instead, each scoring its smallest. What changes?
